title: JavaScript Closures & Scope: The Complete Field Notes
summary: A dense study-notes handbook on how JavaScript decides what a name means and how long it lives — scope chains, var/let/const, hoisting, the temporal dead zone, closures, IIFEs, and the module pattern. Covers the engine mechanics, real-world patterns, memory trade-offs, and the classic bugs each rule was invented to prevent.

chapters.title: Scope: What a Name Means and Where
points: Definition: scope is the region of code where a binding (name → value slot) is resolvable; a binding is the pair, not the value itself.
Three scope kinds in modern JS: global scope, function scope, block scope ({ } — including if/for/while/bare blocks).
Lexical (static) scope: scope is decided by where code is *written*, not where it is *called from* — the engine can resolve names before running.
Contrast with dynamic scope (bash, older Lisps) where a name resolves against the caller's frame — JS never does this; `this` is the only caller-dependent thing.
Scope chain: on lookup, engine checks the innermost scope, then each enclosing scope outward, then global; first match wins, then it stops.
Shadowing: an inner declaration with the same name hides the outer one for the whole inner scope; the outer binding still exists, just unreachable by that name.
Example: `let x = 1; function f() { let x = 2; console.log(x); } f(); console.log(x);` → prints 2 then 1.
ReferenceError: thrown when the chain is exhausted with no match — distinct from `undefined`, which means the binding was found but holds no value.
Global object gotcha: in scripts, top-level `var` and function declarations become properties of `globalThis`; top-level `let`/`const`/`class` do not.
Implicit global: assigning to an undeclared name in sloppy mode creates a global; `'use strict'` turns this into a ReferenceError — one reason to always use strict/modules.
Modules have their own top-level scope: a top-level `var` in an ES module is module-scoped, never global.
Rule of thumb: narrowest scope that works — narrow scope means fewer names alive, fewer collisions, easier reasoning.

chapters.title: var vs let vs const: The Comparison Table
points: Scope row: `var` = function-scoped (ignores blocks); `let`/`const` = block-scoped.
Hoisting row: all three hoist; `var` initializes to `undefined`, `let`/`const` stay uninitialized (TDZ) until the declaration line executes.
Redeclaration row: `var x; var x;` is legal; `let x; let x;` is a SyntaxError at parse time — before any code runs.
Reassignment row: `var` and `let` reassignable; `const` binding is not — `const x = 1; x = 2` throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
Global-object row: top-level `var` attaches to `globalThis`; `let`/`const` live in the script's declarative record, invisible on `globalThis`.
const is not immutability: `const arr = [1,2]; arr.push(3)` is fine — the *binding* is frozen, the object is not. Use `Object.freeze` (shallow) for the value.
`const` requires an initializer: `const x;` is a SyntaxError.
Block leak demo: `if (true) { var a = 1; let b = 2; } console.log(a); // 1` but `console.log(b)` → ReferenceError.
Loop-body semantics: `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration; `var` shares one binding for the whole loop (the source of the classic closure bug).
Mixed-declaration SyntaxError: `var x = 1; let x = 2;` in the same scope is illegal in either order.
Style guidance: `const` by default, `let` when you must rebind, `var` essentially never in new code (keep it for reading legacy).

Function parameters are function-scoped bindings, initialized on call — a `let` of the same name in the body is a SyntaxError, but a `var` of the same name is allowed and reuses the parameter's binding.

chapters.title: Hoisting: What Really Moves
points: Correct model: nothing physically moves — during the creation phase of an execution context, the engine registers all declarations in the scope's environment record before executing any statement.
Function declarations hoist fully (body included): `greet(); function greet(){}` works.
`var` hoists as declaration only, initialized to `undefined`; the assignment stays put and runs in order.
Example: `console.log(x); var x = 5;` → logs `undefined`, not a ReferenceError, not 5.
Function *expressions* do not hoist the body: `f(); var f = function(){}` → TypeError: f is not a function (f is `undefined` when called).
Arrow functions behave like function expressions — the const/let binding is in TDZ, so `f(); const f = () => {}` throws ReferenceError.
`class` declarations hoist but are in TDZ — like `let`, not like `function`.
Precedence: within one scope, function declarations are registered before `var`s; a `var` with the same name does not overwrite the hoisted function unless it is assigned.
Conditional function declarations inside blocks are legal in strict mode but block-scoped — never rely on them; assign a function expression to a `let` instead.
Two-phase mental model to memorize: creation phase (bindings registered, `var`=undefined, `let`/`const`=uninitialized) then execution phase (assignments run top to bottom).
Gotcha: hoisting is per-scope, not per-file — a `var` inside a function is invisible outside it, no matter how it looks.
Practical rule: declare at the top of the scope and hoisting stops being observable, which is the real reason the style rule exists.

chapters.title: The Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
points: Definition: the region from the start of a `let`/`const`/`class` binding's scope up to the line where it is initialized; touching the name there throws.
Exact error: `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization` — distinguishable from `x is not defined` (name never declared at all).
TDZ is temporal, not spatial: it depends on when execution reaches the initializer, not on line position — a function defined above but *called* after the initializer runs fine.
Example: `{ console.log(x); let x = 1; }` → ReferenceError; swap to `var` and it logs `undefined`.
Shadowing trap: `let x = 1; { console.log(x); let x = 2; }` throws — the inner `let` shadows from the block's start, so the outer `x` is unreachable.
`typeof` is not safe for TDZ names: `typeof x` where `x` is a `let` below throws, though `typeof undeclaredName` returns "undefined".
TDZ also applies to function parameters with defaults referencing later params: `function f(a = b, b = 2) {}` → calling `f()` throws.
`const` in TDZ until its initializer runs, which is why `const` can never be observed as `undefined` — a real guarantee you can rely on.
Why it exists: makes use-before-define a loud error instead of a silent `undefined`, and makes `const`'s assign-once guarantee enforceable.
Loop TDZ: in `for (let i = ...)`, each iteration's binding is created fresh and initialized from the previous iteration's copy — the mechanism behind per-iteration capture.
Debug tip: 'Cannot access before initialization' in a bundled file usually means a circular import, not a typo — the module graph evaluated in the wrong order.

chapters.title: Closures: The Core Mechanic
points: Definition: a closure is a function together with the lexical environment in which it was created; the function keeps that environment alive after the outer call returns.
Every JS function is a closure — the term is only interesting when the inner function outlives its creator.
Canonical example: `function counter(){ let c = 0; return () => ++c; } const inc = counter(); inc(); inc(); // 2`.
Closures capture *bindings*, not values — the inner function sees later mutations to the same variable, it does not snapshot at creation.
Proof of binding capture: `let v = 1; const show = () => v; v = 2; show(); // 2`.
Independent instances: each call to the outer function creates a new environment, so two counters from `counter()` do not share state.
Shared instances: two functions returned from the *same* call share one environment — the basis of get/set pairs and private state objects.
Engine mechanics: the environment record moves to the heap (not the discarded stack frame) because a reachable closure holds a reference to it.
Scope chain persistence: the closure holds `[[Environment]]`, an internal pointer to its defining environment record, which chains outward to the global record.
Closures capture the whole environment record, not just the names used — most engines optimize away unreferenced slots, but do not rely on it for large captured objects.
Closures vs objects: both bundle behavior with state; a closure hides state absolutely (unreachable), an object property is always reachable and inspectable.
Loops + closures teaser: `for (var i=0;i<3;i++) setTimeout(()=>console.log(i))` prints 3,3,3 — one shared binding; `let` prints 0,1,2.

chapters.title: The Loop Capture Problem (and Three Fixes)
points: The bug: `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0) }` logs 3, 3, 3.
Why: `var i` is one function-scoped binding; all three callbacks close over the same slot, and by the time the timers fire, the loop has finished and `i` is 3.
Why 3 and not 2: the loop exits only after the increment that fails the condition, so the final stored value is the boundary value.
Fix 1 — `let`: `for (let i = 0; ...)` creates a fresh `i` per iteration; the spec copies the value forward each pass. Logs 0, 1, 2.
Fix 2 — IIFE: `for (var i=0;i<3;i++){ (function(j){ setTimeout(()=>console.log(j)) })(i) }` — the parameter `j` is a new binding per call.
Fix 3 — bind/extra arg: `setTimeout(console.log.bind(null, i), 0)` evaluates `i` at bind time, so the value is frozen into the bound function.
`let` in `for...of`/`for...in` also gets per-iteration bindings; `const` is legal there (no increment to perform) but a SyntaxError in a C-style `for` header.
Same bug with event handlers: attaching handlers in a `var` loop makes every button report the last index.
Same bug with array of functions: `const fns=[]; for(var i=0;i<3;i++) fns.push(()=>i)` — all three return 3.
Non-fix to avoid: `setTimeout("console.log(" + i + ")")` — string eval works by accident, but is slow, unsafe, and breaks minification.
Async variant: an `await` inside a `var` loop shows the same aliasing; per-iteration `let` also fixes it.
Takeaway to memorize: the closure is never 'late' — the variable simply changed. Fix the binding, not the timing.

chapters.title: IIFE: Immediately Invoked Function Expressions
points: Form: `(function(){ /* ... */ })();` — wrap in parens to force expression position, then call immediately.
Why the wrapper is needed: a statement starting with `function` is parsed as a declaration, and a declaration cannot be immediately invoked.
Alternative unary-operator forms: `!function(){}()`, `+function(){}()`, `void function(){}()` — all coerce to expression position; the paren form is the readable default.
Second call-paren style: `(function(){}())` — Crockford's placement; identical behavior, purely a style choice.
Arrow IIFE: `(() => { ... })()` — shorter, but has no own `this`/`arguments`, so it cannot replace an IIFE used for `this` capture.
Async IIFE: `(async () => { await main() })()` — the standard way to use `await` at the top level of a CommonJS file or a script without top-level await.
Primary historical purpose: create a private function scope in an era when `var` was the only declaration and everything else leaked to global.
Parameter injection for safety and minification: `(function($, undefined){ ... })(jQuery)` — pins globals to locals and guarantees `undefined` really is undefined.
Return-value IIFE: `const config = (function(){ /* compute */ return result })()` — run setup once, keep only the result in scope.
ASI hazard: a line before an IIFE that lacks a semicolon makes the parser read `(` as a call on the previous expression — the reason for the defensive leading `;(function(){})()`.
Modern status: a bare block `{ let x = 1 }` gives block privacy, and ES modules give file privacy — IIFEs are now mostly for async top-level and once-only setup.
Bundlers still emit IIFEs: the IIFE output format wraps a whole bundle so its internals never touch the page's global scope.

chapters.title: The Module Pattern: Privacy Built From Closures
points: Classic module pattern: an IIFE holds private state and returns an object of public methods that close over it.
Example: `const store = (function(){ let items = []; return { add(x){ items.push(x) }, count(){ return items.length } } })();` — `items` is unreachable from outside.
Revealing module pattern variant: declare everything as inner functions, then return a map of names to those functions — one place to read the public surface.
True privacy: closure-private state cannot be reached by `Object.keys`, bracket access, JSON serialization, or a debugger's property inspector.
Singleton by construction: the IIFE runs once, so the module pattern yields exactly one instance; wrap in a factory function instead if you need many.
Factory form: `function makeStore(){ let items = []; return { add, count } }` — one private environment per call, the closure-based alternative to `class`.
Comparison with `class` + `#private` fields: `#` fields give real privacy with prototype-based method sharing; closures allocate fresh function objects per instance.
Memory trade-off: N closure-based instances create N copies of each method; N class instances share one prototype method — measurable at large N.
Augmentation pattern: `const app = (function(m){ m.newFeature = ...; return m })(app || {})` — how pre-ES6 libraries split a module across files.
Namespacing motive: before modules, everything shared one global — the pattern existed to expose exactly one name.
Relationship to ES modules: `import`/`export` gives the same privacy at file granularity, statically analyzable and tree-shakeable — prefer it in new code.
ES module live bindings: an imported name is a live view of the exporter's binding, not a copied value — closer to closure capture than to assignment.

chapters.title: Closures in Practice: The Standard Patterns
points: Data privacy / encapsulation: bank-account style `deposit`/`getBalance` pair with no way to set the balance directly.
Function factories: `const multiplier = n => x => x * n; const double = multiplier(2)` — the returned function closes over `n`.
Partial application and currying: `const add = a => b => a + b; add(1)(2)` — each layer captures its argument.
Memoization: `function memo(fn){ const cache = new Map(); return x => cache.has(x) ? cache.get(x) : (cache.set(x, fn(x)), cache.get(x)) }` — the cache lives in the closure.
Debounce: closure holds the pending `timeoutId` across calls so a new call can clear the previous timer.
Throttle: closure holds `lastRun` timestamp to gate execution frequency.
Once: `function once(fn){ let done = false, val; return (...a) => done ? val : (done = true, val = fn(...a)) }`.
Rate/attempt counters and ID generators: `const nextId = (() => { let i = 0; return () => ++i })()`.
React `useState`/`useEffect` closures: a stale-closure bug happens when an effect captures an old render's state; the deps array controls which closure is live.
Event handler with captured context: attaching `el.addEventListener('click', () => handle(item))` inside a `map` — each handler closes over its own `item`.
Iterator/generator-free lazy sequences: a closure over a cursor variable gives a `next()` without generator syntax.
Callback context in async code: closures are why a `.then()` callback can still see the variables from the function that started the request.

chapters.title: Memory, Performance, and Leaks
points: Cost model: a closure keeps its whole captured environment record alive; it is garbage-collected only when every closure referencing it is unreachable.
Leak pattern 1 — long-lived listener: a handler registered on a global/DOM node capturing a big object keeps that object alive until `removeEventListener`.
Leak pattern 2 — detached DOM node: a closure holding an element reference prevents GC of that element and its entire subtree even after removal from the document.
Leak pattern 3 — unbounded memo cache: closure-held `Map` grows forever; fix with an LRU bound or `WeakMap` keyed by object.
`WeakMap`/`WeakRef`: hold keys weakly so the entry disappears when the key is collected — the tool for caches attached to objects.
Shared-environment surprise: two closures from one call share the environment, so a small surviving closure can pin a large variable captured by its sibling.
Mitigation: null out large captured references (`bigData = null`) when done, or restructure so the big value is captured in a narrower inner scope.
Performance: variable lookup cost grows with scope-chain depth; engines cache and often inline, so this is rarely the bottleneck — measure before restructuring.
Allocation cost: creating a closure inside a hot loop allocates a function object per iteration; hoist the function out if it captures nothing loop-specific.
`eval` and `with` defeat static scope analysis and force the engine into a slow deoptimized path for the entire enclosing function.
Diagnosing: Chrome DevTools heap snapshot → 'Retainers' / 'Closure' entries show which closure context holds a leaked object.
Trade-off summary: closures buy encapsulation and per-instance state at the price of heap-allocated environments and a longer object lifetime than the call.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and How to Read the Errors
points: Assuming closures snapshot values — they capture bindings; the classic loop bug and React stale-closure bug are the same mistake.
Assuming `const` means deep immutability — it freezes the binding only; mutating a `const` object is legal.
Using `typeof` as a TDZ guard — it throws for `let`/`const` in the TDZ, unlike for truly undeclared names.
Forgetting that `var` ignores blocks: a `var` inside `if`/`for` is visible for the whole function and can silently clobber an earlier value.
Accidental globals in sloppy mode: a missing `let` in `for (i = 0; ...)` creates a global `i` that other code can trample.
Circular imports producing 'Cannot access X before initialization' — a module-graph ordering problem, not a scope typo.
`this` is not lexically scoped in normal functions — losing `this` in a callback is a separate problem from closures; fix with an arrow function or `bind`.
Error message decoder: `x is not defined` = never declared; `Cannot access 'x' before initialization` = declared but in TDZ; `x is undefined` (as a value) = declared and hoisted `var`, or unassigned.
`Assignment to constant variable` = reassigning a `const` binding, not mutating its contents.
`Identifier 'x' has already been declared` = duplicate `let`/`const`/mixed with `var` in one scope — a parse-time error, so nothing in the file runs.
Redeclaring a parameter with `let` in the function body → SyntaxError; a common surprise when refactoring.
Debug checklist: (1) which scope declares the name, (2) is it a binding or a value that changed, (3) when did the capturing function actually run.

chapters.title: Summary: The Rules Worth Memorizing
points: Scope is lexical — decided by where code is written; only `this` depends on the call site.
Lookup walks the chain inward-to-outward and stops at the first match; no match = ReferenceError.
`var` is function-scoped and hoists to `undefined`; `let`/`const` are block-scoped and hoist into the TDZ.
Default to `const`, use `let` when rebinding, treat `var` as read-only legacy.
Every function closes over its defining environment; that environment survives as long as the function does.
Closures capture bindings, not values — the #1 source of loop and stale-state bugs.
`let` in a loop header gives one fresh binding per iteration; `var` gives one shared binding for all.
IIFEs were the pre-ES6 way to make a private scope; today use blocks, modules, or an async IIFE for top-level `await`.
The module pattern = IIFE + closure + returned public object; it gives real privacy and a singleton by default.
Closure-per-instance costs memory (methods duplicated, environment heap-allocated); classes with `#private` share methods via the prototype.
Watch for leaks where a closure outlives its usefulness: listeners, detached DOM nodes, unbounded caches.
One-line mental model: a closure is a function that remembers where it was born, not where it was called.
